mainTopic: How carefully must a שומר שכר guard, and which attacks count as אונס for him?
overview: רבה rules that a שומר שכר who guarded the way people normally guard is exempt. That includes going into town or napping at the usual times. אביי challenges him with ברייתות about an armed raid, about יעקב's guarding through heat and frost, and about a shepherd who left for town. רבה answers each one: city guards (חזני מתא) have a higher duty, יעקב did extra, and a shepherd who fled a lion must still gather help. A שומר חנם must use free help, while a שומר שכר must hire help up to the animals' value, and the owner pays him back. רב חסדא and רבה בר רב הונא disagree with רבה and hold that a paid watchman is paid for extra guarding. Two stories follow, a porter on a narrow bridge and flax snatched by a robber, and in both the watchman is held liable. A new משנה then lists which attacks count as אונס: one wolf versus two, dogs, bandits, wild beasts, and losses the shepherd caused himself. The גמרא explains that the bandits are armed, rules that even an armed shepherd need not fight an armed bandit, and begins אביי's case of a shepherd who taunts a thief, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: רבה's reason: he guarded the normal way
steps.stepSummary: רבה explains why the shepherd is exempt: he guarded the way people normally guard.
steps.simpleTranslation: After all, he guarded the way people usually guard.
steps.whatsHappening: This line finishes רבה's ruling from just before. It gives his reason why the shepherd is not responsible for the attack.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה's standard is normal human behavior. A paid watchman only has to guard the way ordinary people guard, and anything beyond that is not required of him. Everything that follows tests how far this standard goes.
steps.whatToRemember: רבה's rule: a שומר שכר who guarded the normal way is exempt.

phrases.english: After all, he guarded the way people guard.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רבה's ruling from the previous section by giving its reason.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A paid watchman who guarded in the normal, accepted way is exempt.

steps.title: אביי asks: going into town at the usual time
steps.stepSummary: אביי pushes רבה's logic: would a shepherd who went into town when shepherds normally do also be exempt?
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: If so, if he went into town at the time when people go in, would he also be exempt?!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי takes רבה's rule and tests it on a surprising case, a shepherd who leaves the flock to go into town.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If 'normal guarding' is enough, then leaving the flock at a normal time should also be fine. אביי expects this result to sound too lenient. He is trying to show that רבה's rule goes too far.

keyTerms.meaning: if so, then... (introduces a challenge from the logic just stated)

phrases.english: אביי said to him:
If that is so,
if he went into town at the time when people go in –
is he also exempt?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests רבה's reason on a more extreme case.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's rule that normal guarding is enough.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: By that logic, leaving the flock to go to town at the normal time would also exempt him, which seems too lenient.

steps.title: רבה: Yes, he is exempt
steps.stepSummary: רבה accepts the result: going into town at the normal time is also exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Yes.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה does not back down. He agrees that this shepherd is exempt too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of avoiding the challenge, רבה accepts its conclusion. Since shepherds normally go into town at that hour, doing so counts as normal guarding.

phrases.english: He said to him: Yes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אביי's challenge by accepting it.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: אביי assumed that leaving for town must make a watchman liable.
steps.terutzMaskana: Going into town at the normal time is also normal guarding, so he is exempt.

steps.title: אביי asks: napping at the usual time
steps.stepSummary: אביי pushes further: would a watchman who dozed off when people normally sleep also be exempt?
steps.simpleTranslation: If he slept a little at the time when people sleep, would he also be exempt?!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי tries an even stronger case, a watchman who takes a short nap.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sleeping on the job sounds worse than going into town. אביי wants to see whether רבה will stretch 'normal behavior' this far.

phrases.english: If he slept a little
at the time when people sleep –
is he also exempt?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, stronger test of the same rule.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's rule that normal guarding is enough.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: By that logic, even napping at a normal hour would be exempt, which seems hard to accept.

steps.title: רבה: Yes, he is exempt here too
steps.stepSummary: רבה again accepts the result: napping at the normal time is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Yes.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה holds firm again and agrees that the napping watchman is exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה stays consistent. Whatever people normally do counts as proper guarding, even a short nap. Now אביי will bring actual sources to argue against him.
steps.whatToRemember: רבה holds that going into town or napping at normal times is still proper guarding, so the watchman is exempt.

phrases.english: He said to him: Yes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the second challenge by accepting it.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Sleeping on duty must surely make a watchman liable.
steps.terutzMaskana: A nap at a normal time is still normal guarding, so he is exempt.

steps.title: Objection from the raid of שבא
steps.stepSummary: אביי quotes a ברייתא showing that only something as severe as an armed raid exempts a שומר שכר.
steps.simpleTranslation: He challenged him: These are the accidents for which a paid watchman is exempt, for example: 'שבא attacked and took them, and struck the servants with the sword.'
steps.whatsHappening: אביי now brings a ברייתא as a source against רבה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא gives an armed raid as its example of an אונס. That suggests only something that big exempts a paid watchman. A wolf attack while he was in town would not be enough, against רבה.

phrases.english: He challenged him: These are the accidents
for which a paid watchman is exempt –
for example: 'And Sheva attacked and took them,
and struck the servants with the edge of the sword.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵיתִיבֵיהּ: אֵלּוּ הֵם אוֹנָסִין שֶׁשּׁוֹמֵר שָׂכָר פָּטוּר עֲלֵיהֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from logical tests to a source-based challenge.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's rule that normal guarding exempts the watchman.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If only an armed raid counts as an אונס, smaller events like a wolf attack while he was away should make him liable.

steps.title: רבה: That is about city guards
steps.stepSummary: רבה answers that the ברייתא is talking about professional city guards, who have a higher duty.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: There it is talking about city guards.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה limits the ברייתא to a special kind of watchman.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Professional city guards (חזני מתא) are hired to guard at a much higher level. For them, only something like an armed raid is an excuse. An ordinary paid watchman still only needs normal guarding.

phrases.english: He said to him: There it is about city guards.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defends רבה against the first ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the source to a specific case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא sets the standard for every paid watchman.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא only describes professional city guards, who have a stricter duty.

steps.title: Objection from יעקב's heat and frost
steps.stepSummary: אביי quotes a ברייתא that sets יעקב אבינו's day-and-night guarding as the standard for a paid watchman.
steps.simpleTranslation: He challenged him: How far must a paid watchman guard? To the point of 'By day the heat consumed me, and the frost by night.'
steps.whatsHappening: אביי brings a second ברייתא against רבה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This ברייתא says a paid watchman must guard like יעקב did, through burning heat and freezing nights. That leaves no room for naps or trips into town, which contradicts רבה.

phrases.english: He challenged him: Until what point
is a paid watchman obligated to guard?
To the point of: 'Thus I was: by day the heat consumed me,
and the frost by night.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵיתִיבֵיהּ: עַד מָתַי שׁוֹמֵר שָׂכָר חַיָּיב לִשְׁמוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second source-based challenge to רבה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's rule that normal guarding is enough.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The required standard is round-the-clock guarding through heat and cold, so a normal nap or trip to town should not be allowed.

steps.title: רבה: That is also about city guards
steps.stepSummary: רבה gives the same answer: this ברייתא is also about professional city guards.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: There too it is talking about city guards.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה uses his earlier answer again for the second ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The extreme standard of heat and frost applies only to professional guards. An ordinary paid watchman is still judged by normal guarding.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הָתָם נָמֵי בְּחַזָּנֵי מָתָא.
phrases.english: He said to him: There too it is about city guards.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הָתָם נָמֵי בְּחַזָּנֵי מָתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the answer from step 7 to the second ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the source to a specific case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: יעקב's standard applies to every paid watchman.
steps.terutzMaskana: It applies only to professional city guards.

steps.title: אביי: Was יעקב a city guard?
steps.stepSummary: אביי objects that יעקב אבינו was a shepherd, not a city guard, so his verse cannot be about city guards.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Was יעקב אבינו a city guard?!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי attacks רבה's last answer directly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא learns its rule from יעקב, who was an ordinary hired shepherd for לבן. So his standard should apply to ordinary paid watchmen, and רבה's limit to city guards seems not to fit.

keyTerms.meaning: is that to say...? (a disbelieving question)

phrases.english: He said to him: Was יעקב אבינו, then,
a city guard?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אַטּוּ יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ חַזַּן מָתָא הֲוָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's claim that the יעקב ברייתא is about city guards.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: יעקב was a regular hired shepherd, so a rule learned from him must apply to regular paid watchmen.

steps.title: רבה: יעקב did extra, like a city guard
steps.stepSummary: רבה explains that יעקב was telling לבן he had guarded far beyond what was required, at the level of a city guard.
steps.simpleTranslation: For he said to לבן: I guarded for you with extra guarding, like city guards.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה explains what יעקב meant, which keeps his answer standing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: יעקב's words were not describing the basic duty of a shepherd. He was telling לבן that he had gone above and beyond, guarding like a professional city guard. So the basic duty of an ordinary paid watchman is still just normal guarding.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't read יעקב's heat-and-frost guarding as the legal minimum. According to רבה, it was extra effort beyond what the law requires.

phrases.english: For he said to לבן:
I guarded for you with extra guarding,
like city guards.

steps.triggerLanguage: דַּאֲמַר לֵיהּ לְלָבָן: נְטַרִי לָךְ נְטִירוּתָא יַתִּירְתָּא כְּחַזָּנֵי מָתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אביי's challenge about יעקב.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: יעקב's words describe the basic duty of a hired shepherd.
steps.terutzMaskana: יעקב was describing extra guarding, at the level of city guards, beyond the basic duty.
steps.whyThisMatters: This keeps רבה's standard intact: an ordinary paid watchman only needs to guard the normal way.

steps.title: Objection from the shepherd who left for town
steps.stepSummary: אביי quotes a ברייתא about a shepherd who left his flock and went to town. The court estimates whether he could have saved the animals, and if so he is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: He challenged him: A shepherd who was herding, and left his flock and came to town, and a wolf came and tore or a lion came and trampled, we do not say 'Had he been there he would have saved them.' Rather we estimate: if he could have saved them, he is liable. If not, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי brings a third ברייתא, which seems to match רבה's case exactly. Steps 13 to 20 work through how רבה answers it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This ברייתא describes a shepherd who left for town, which is just what רבה said is exempt. Yet it says he is liable if he could have saved the animals. So it seems that going to town is not automatically normal guarding.

phrases.english: He challenged him: A shepherd who was herding
and left his flock and came to town,
and a wolf came and tore,
or a lion came and trampled –
we do not say:
'Had he been there, he would have saved them.'
Rather, we estimate about him:
if he could have saved them – he is liable,
if not – he is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵיתִיבֵיהּ: רוֹעֶה שֶׁהָיָה רוֹעֶה וְהִנִּיחַ עֶדְרוֹ וּבָא לָעִיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third source-based challenge, this time on the exact case of going into town.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's ruling in step 3 that going into town at the normal time is exempt.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא makes a shepherd who left for town liable whenever he could have saved the animals, so leaving is not automatically proper guarding.

steps.title: Isn't the ברייתא talking about a normal time to go to town?
steps.stepSummary: אביי finishes his challenge: the ברייתא seems to be about a shepherd who went to town when people usually go, and it still holds him responsible.
steps.simpleTranslation: Isn't this ברייתא talking about a shepherd who went into town at a time when people normally go in?
steps.whatsHappening: אביי completes the challenge he started in Step 12. He reads the ברייתא as a case where the shepherd left at a normal hour.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה holds that a שומר שכר does not have to guard beyond what is normal. If the ברייתא makes the shepherd liable even when he left at a normal hour, he had to guard beyond the normal standard, and that goes against רבה.

keyTerms.meaning: Isn't it that...? (a lead-in to a challenge)

phrases.english: Isn't it that he went in
at a time when people go in?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי לָאו דְּעָל בְּעִידָּנָא דְּעָיְילִי אִינָשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the challenge from the ברייתא quoted in Step 12
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's view that a שומר שכר only has to guard at the normal level
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If he left at a normal hour and is still liable when he could have saved the animals, then extra guarding is required.

steps.title: No, he went in at an unusual time
steps.stepSummary: רבה answers that the ברייתא is about a shepherd who went to town when people do not usually go.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is talking about someone who went in at a time when people do not normally go in.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה narrows the ברייתא to a shepherd who left at an odd hour.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Leaving at an unusual time is already below the normal standard of guarding. So the liability in the ברייתא does not prove that guarding beyond normal is required.

keyTerms.meaning: when they do not go in

phrases.english: No, it is where he went in
at a time when people do not go in.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא, דְּעָל בְּעִידָּנָא דְּלָא עָיְילִי אִינָשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 13 by changing the case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא is about leaving at a normal hour.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is about leaving at an unusual hour, which is already careless.

steps.title: Then why is he ever exempt?
steps.stepSummary: אביי objects: if he left at an odd hour, he was careless from the start, so he should be liable even when the animals could not have been saved.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why is he exempt when he could not have saved them? It started with carelessness and ended with an accident, so he should be liable!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי attacks רבה's new reading. The ברייתא says that if the shepherd could not have saved the animals he is exempt, and that does not fit a shepherd who was careless.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When a loss starts with carelessness and ends in an accident (תחילתו בפשיעה וסופו באונס), the watchman is liable. Leaving at an odd hour is careless, so the exemption in the ברייתא makes no sense under רבה's reading.

keyTerms.meaning: If so (introducing a problem with the last answer)
It started with carelessness and ended in an accident

steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא has two halves: liable if he could have saved them, exempt if he couldn't. אביי is attacking the exempt half here.

phrases.english: If so, why is he exempt?
Its beginning was through carelessness
and its end through an accident, so he is liable!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבה's answer in Step 14
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's reading that the shepherd left at an unusual time
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A careless start makes him liable even for an accidental ending, so the ברייתא's exemption can't fit.

steps.title: He heard a lion and ran into town
steps.stepSummary: רבה explains that the shepherd went in because he heard a lion roar, so leaving was not careless.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is where he heard the sound of a lion and went in.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה gives a new picture of the case: the shepherd fled to town out of fear of a lion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Running away from a lion is not carelessness; he had no real choice. So the start was not פשיעה, and the exemption when he couldn't have saved the animals makes sense again.

phrases.english: It is where he heard the sound of a lion and went in.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 15 by refining the case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Leaving at an odd hour means he was careless.
steps.terutzMaskana: He left because of a lion, which is forced, not careless.

steps.title: What could he have done against a lion?
steps.stepSummary: אביי asks why the court would need to estimate anything. Against a lion, what could the shepherd possibly have done?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why do they estimate about him? What could he have done?!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי challenges the lion case. The ברייתא says the court estimates whether he could have saved the animals, but against a lion there seems to be nothing to estimate.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a lion attacked, the loss looks like a pure accident. Then the ברייתא's line about the court estimating whether he could have saved them seems pointless.

keyTerms.meaning: the court estimates about him (whether he could have saved them)

phrases.english: If so, do they estimate about him?
What should he have done?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the lion case from Step 16
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Against a lion nothing can be done, so the ברייתא's estimate has no purpose.

steps.title: He should have faced it with shepherds and sticks
steps.stepSummary: רבה answers that the shepherd could have gathered other shepherds with sticks to chase the lion away.
steps.simpleTranslation: He should have gone out against it with shepherds and sticks.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה explains what the court is estimating: whether he could have gathered help to drive off the lion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even a lion can sometimes be scared off by a group of shepherds with sticks. The court estimates whether such help was available. If it was, he is liable; if not, he is exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: to go out to meet / confront

phrases.english: He should have gone out to face it
with shepherds and with sticks.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 17
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Nothing can be done against a lion.
steps.terutzMaskana: He could have gathered shepherds with sticks, and the court checks whether that was possible.

steps.title: Why only a paid watchman? An unpaid one is also liable
steps.stepSummary: אביי asks why the ברייתא speaks of a שומר שכר, when רבה himself said that even a שומר חנם who could have gathered shepherds and sticks is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why mention specifically a paid watchman? Even an unpaid watchman is the same, since you, Master, said: an unpaid watchman who could have faced it with shepherds and sticks and didn't is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי uses רבה's own earlier ruling against him. If the rule is about gathering shepherds, it applies to a שומר חנם too, so why does the ברייתא single out a שומר שכר?
steps.deeperAnalysis: A שומר חנם is only liable for carelessness, and רבה said failing to gather help counts as carelessness even for him. So a rule about gathering help adds nothing special for a שומר שכר.

phrases.aramaic: אִי הָכִי, מַאי אִירְיָא שׁוֹמֵר שָׂכָר?
phrases.english: If so, why specifically a paid watchman?
Even an unpaid watchman too,
for it was the Master himself who said:
phrases.notes: אביי is talking to רבה, his teacher, so 'the Master' means רבה himself.

phrases.english: An unpaid watchman who could have gone out to face it
with shepherds and sticks and did not face it is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, מַאי אִירְיָא שׁוֹמֵר שָׂכָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges Step 18 using רבה's own earlier statement
steps.kashyaTarget: The explanation that the estimate is about gathering shepherds and sticks
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: That duty already applies to a שומר חנם, so the ברייתא's focus on a שומר שכר would be pointless.

steps.title: Unpaid gets free help, paid must hire help
steps.stepSummary: רבה answers: a שומר חנם must gather help only when it is free; a שומר שכר must gather help even if he has to pay for it.
steps.simpleTranslation: An unpaid watchman, with free help; a paid watchman, even with paid help.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה shows the difference between the two watchmen. Both must gather help, but only the paid watchman has to hire it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So the ברייתא does teach something special about a שומר שכר: he must spend money to hire helpers. A שומר חנם is only liable if free help was available and he didn't use it.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets a practical difference between the two kinds of watchmen when animals are under attack.

phrases.english: An unpaid watchman, with free help;
a paid watchman, even with paid help.

steps.triggerLanguage: שׁוֹמֵר חִנָּם בְּחִנָּם, שׁוֹמֵר שָׂכָר בְּשָׂכָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 19
steps.terutzResolutionType: Drawing a distinction between the two watchmen
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both watchmen have the same duty to gather help.
steps.terutzMaskana: The paid watchman must hire help; the unpaid one only uses free help.

steps.title: How much must he spend on hiring help?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the limit is on what a שומר שכר must spend to hire helpers.
steps.simpleTranslation: And up to how much?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא follows up on רבה's rule with a question: how much money does the paid watchman have to spend?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once he must pay for help, there needs to be a limit. This question sets up the answer in the next step.

phrases.english: And up to how much?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the limit of the rule in Step 20
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The maximum a שומר שכר must spend on hired help

steps.title: Up to the value of the animals
steps.stepSummary: The answer: he must spend up to the value of the animals he is guarding.
steps.simpleTranslation: Up to their value.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the limit: he must spend as much as the animals are worth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: It makes no sense to spend more than the animals are worth to save them. So the cap is their full value.

phrases.english: Up to their value.
phrases.notes: 'Their' means the animals he is guarding.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 21
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He must spend up to the value of the animals.

steps.title: But a paid watchman isn't liable for accidents
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: making him pay for help against a lion is like making a שומר שכר pay for an אונס, and where do we ever find that?
steps.simpleTranslation: But where do we find that a paid watchman is liable for accidents?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the rule. A lion attack is an accident (אונס), and a שומר שכר is not responsible for accidents.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he must spend his own money up to the animals' value, he is really carrying the loss from an accident. That goes against the basic rule that a שומר שכר is exempt from אונסין.

phrases.english: And where have we found regarding a paid watchman
that he is liable for accidents?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהֵיכָן מָצִינוּ בְּשׁוֹמֵר שָׂכָר שֶׁחַיָּיב בָּאוֹנָסִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the rule from Steps 20 and 22
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that a שומר שכר must spend up to the animals' value on help
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Paying for protection from a lion means he carries the cost of an accident, but a שומר שכר is exempt from אונסין.

steps.title: He gets the money back from the owner
steps.stepSummary: The answer: the watchman pays for the help, but then collects that money back from the owner.
steps.simpleTranslation: He goes back and takes their cost from the owner.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the problem: the watchman lays out the money, but the owner pays him back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The watchman's duty is only to arrange and pay for the help at the moment of danger. In the end the cost falls on the owner, so the שומר שכר never actually pays for an accident.
steps.whatToRemember: A שומר שכר must hire help to protect the animals, up to their value, but the owner pays him back. A שומר חנם only has to use help that is free.
steps.whyThisMatters: This keeps the basic rule that a שומר שכר is not liable for אונסין, while still requiring him to act when the animals are in danger.

phrases.english: He goes back and takes their cost
phrases.notes: Here 'their cost' means what he paid the helpers.

phrases.english: from the owner.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 23
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shifting the final cost to the owner
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The watchman ends up paying for an accident.
steps.terutzMaskana: He only pays up front; the owner pays him back.

steps.title: What does the owner gain if he pays for the helpers?
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא challenges אביי: if the owner has to pay back the cost of the helpers, what benefit does he get from the rule?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said to אביי: If so, what does the owner gain from this?
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא pushes back on the answer in step 24, that the owner pays back what the watchman spent on helpers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the owner pays the helpers up to the value of his animals, he seems to lose the same amount he would have lost to the lion. So the rule looks pointless for him. רב פפא wants to know what the owner actually gains.

keyTerms.meaning: If so (if that is the rule)
What good does it do him?

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said to Abaye:
If so,
what benefit does he get from it?
phrases.notes: "He" is the owner of the animals.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, מַאי אַהֲנִי לֵיהּ מִינַּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the point of the answer in step 24
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that the owner pays back the watchman's cost of hiring helpers
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the owner pays up to the animals' value, he gains nothing compared to simply losing the animals

steps.title: The owner keeps his own familiar animals and avoids extra bother
steps.stepSummary: The answer: the owner gains because he keeps his own good, familiar animals, or because he saves himself the trouble of getting new ones.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes a difference for the quality of the animals. Or else, it saves extra effort.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers רב פפא with two reasons why the owner still gains, even though he pays for the helpers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if the money comes out the same, the owner keeps the specific animals he knows and trusts. Also, buying new animals takes time and work. So saving his own animals is worth it to him.

keyTerms.meaning: The practical difference that comes out of it
The fitness or good quality of the animals

steps.whatToRemember: A שומר שכר must hire help to save the animals, up to their value. The owner pays him back, and he still gains by keeping his own animals and avoiding extra trouble.

phrases.english: The difference is for the fitness of the animals.
phrases.notes: He keeps the animals he already knows are good, rather than buying unknown ones.

phrases.english: Alternatively, for the extra effort.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב פפא's challenge
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The owner gains nothing, since he pays the full value anyway
steps.terutzMaskana: The owner gains by keeping his familiar, good animals and avoiding the bother of getting new ones

steps.title: Some hold that a paid watchman must guard with extra care
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא and רבה בר רב הונא disagree with רבה. They hold that the owner pays the שומר שכר precisely so that he guards with extra care.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא and רבה בר רב הונא do not agree with רבה, because they say: This is why I paid you, so that you would guard for me with extra care.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings two אמוראים who disagree with רבה about how carefully a paid watchman must guard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה holds that even a שומר שכר only needs to guard in the normal way. רב חסדא and רבה בר רב הונא say the payment itself is for guarding above the normal level. This raises the standard for a paid watchman.

keyTerms.meaning: They do not hold this view
Extra guarding, a higher level of watching

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets out two views on how much care a שומר שכר owes. The stories that follow show watchmen held to a high standard.

phrases.aramaic: רַב חִסְדָּא וְרַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא
phrases.english: Rav Chisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna
do not hold this view of Rabba,
for they say:
For this I gave you a wage,
so that you guard for me with extra guarding.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Presents an opposing view to רבה's approach
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A שומר שכר is paid to guard with extra care, beyond the normal level

steps.title: A porter's animal falls off a narrow bridge, and רב פפא holds him liable
steps.stepSummary: בר אדא the porter was leading animals across a narrow bridge. One pushed another into the water. רב פפא held him liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: בר אדא the porter was leading animals across the narrow bridge of נרש. One pushed another and threw it into the water. He came before רב פפא, who held him liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story about a hired porter who lost an animal, and רב פפא ruled that he must pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The loss looks almost like an accident (אונס), since one animal pushed another. Still, רב פפא held the porter liable. The next steps explain why.

keyTerms.meaning: A porter, someone hired to carry or move things
He held him liable (he must pay)

phrases.english: Bar Adda the porter
was transporting animals
phrases.notes: Some versions have the round-bracket word and some have the square-bracket word. Both mean "was."

phrases.english: across the narrow bridge of Neresh.
One pushed its companion
and threw it into the water.
He came before Rav Pappa, who held him liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: בַּר אַדָּא סָבוֹלָאָה הֲוָה קָא מְעַבַּר חֵיוָתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A story showing a hired watchman held to a high standard
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The porter is liable for the animal that was pushed off the bridge

steps.title: The porter asks what else he could have done
steps.stepSummary: בר אדא protests: what should I have done?
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: What should I have done?
steps.whatsHappening: The porter challenges the ruling by saying he had no way to stop it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He is arguing that this was an accident beyond his control, so he should be exempt.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מַאי הֲוָה לִי לְמֶעְבַּד?
phrases.english: He said to him: What should I have done?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב פפא's ruling
steps.kashyaTarget: רב פפא's ruling that the porter is liable
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: There was nothing he could have done, so it was an accident

steps.title: You should have led them across one at a time
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא answers that he should have taken the animals across one by one.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: You should have taken them across one at a time.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא tells the porter there was something he could have done.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Taking the animals across one at a time would have stopped them from pushing each other. So the loss came from his lack of care, and it was not a true accident.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִבְּעִי לָךְ לְעַבּוֹרֵי חֲדָא חֲדָא.
phrases.english: He said to him: You should have taken them across one by one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the porter's protest
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The loss was a pure accident
steps.terutzMaskana: He could have prevented it by leading them one at a time, so he is negligent

steps.title: The porter says nobody can do that
steps.stepSummary: The porter objects: do you know anyone, even your own nephew, who can take animals across one by one?
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Do you know of your sister's son who can take them across one by one?
steps.whatsHappening: The porter pushes back again and says that crossing one by one is not realistic.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He is saying the demand is too much. No porter actually works that way, so it should not count as negligence.

keyTerms.meaning: Your sister's son, your nephew (a way of saying "anyone at all")

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: יָדְעַתְּ בֵּיהּ בְּבַר אֲחָתָיךְ
phrases.english: He said to him: Do you know of your sister's son
phrases.notes: This is a figure of speech meaning "do you know of anyone at all."

phrases.english: who can take them across one by one?
phrases.notes: Some versions have the extra letter in round brackets and some leave it out. The meaning stays the same.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב פפא's answer
steps.kashyaTarget: The demand to lead the animals one at a time
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Nobody can realistically do that, so it is not a fair standard

steps.title: This complaint is old, and no one ever accepted it
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא answers that people before him already raised this complaint, and nobody paid attention to it.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Those before you already cried out about this, and no one paid attention to them.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא rejects the porter's excuse and keeps his ruling. The porter is liable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The claim that it is too hard is not new, and it was never accepted as an excuse. A hired porter is held to the careful standard, so he must pay.
steps.whatToRemember: A hired porter who could have prevented a loss by being more careful is liable, even if the extra care is hard.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: כְּבָר צְוַוחוּ קַמָּאֵי דְקַמָּךְ
phrases.english: He said to him: Those before you already cried out
and there was no one who paid attention to them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the porter's second protest and ends the story
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rejects the excuse as long dismissed
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Because the extra care is hard, the porter should be exempt
steps.terutzMaskana: The excuse was never accepted, so the porter stays liable

steps.title: Flax snatched by a robber, and רב נחמן holds the watchman liable
steps.stepSummary: אייבו left flax with רוניא. A robber named שבו snatched it. Later the thief was identified, and רב נחמן held the watchman liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: אייבו deposited flax in the house of רוניא. שבו came and snatched it from him. In the end the thief was identified. He came before רב נחמן, who held him liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a second story, about a watchman who lost an item to a robber and was still held liable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being robbed is normally treated as an accident (אונס), which a watchman does not pay for. Yet רב נחמן held this watchman liable. The detail that the thief was identified seems to matter.

phrases.english: Aivu deposited flax in the house of Ronya.
Shabbu went and snatched it from him.
phrases.notes: שבו is the robber, and "him" is רוניא, the watchman.

phrases.english: In the end the thief was identified.
He came before Rav Nachman, who held him liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second story about a watchman held liable
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The watchman is liable for the flax snatched by a robber who was later identified

steps.title: Does רב נחמן disagree with רב הונא בר אבין?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether רב נחמן's ruling conflicts with a ruling of רב הונא בר אבין.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say that this disagrees with רב הונא בר אבין?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move. It asks whether רב נחמן's ruling clashes with what רב הונא בר אבין taught.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words "shall we say" suggest a possible conflict between the two rulings. The גמרא will now bring רב הונא בר אבין's teaching and work out whether they really disagree.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say? (often opens a suggestion the גמרא may reject)

steps.confusionAlert: "לֵימָא" opens a suggestion, not a final ruling. The גמרא often goes on to show that there is no real disagreement.

phrases.aramaic: לֵימָא פְּלִיגָא דְּרַב הוּנָא בַּר אָבִין?
phrases.english: Shall we say it disagrees with Rav Huna bar Avin?

steps.triggerLanguage: לֵימָא פְּלִיגָא דְּרַב הוּנָא בַּר אָבִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions how רב נחמן's ruling fits with another אמורא's ruling
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן's ruling holding the watchman liable
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: It appears to conflict with a ruling of רב הונא בר אבין

steps.title: רב הונא בר אבין's ruling on a stolen item when the thief is found
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes רב הונא בר אבין: if an item was taken by force and the thief is later found, a שׁוֹמֵר חִנָּם may choose to swear or to sue the thief. A שׁוֹמֵר שָׂכָר must sue the thief and does not swear.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רב הונא בר אבין sent: if it was stolen by force and later the thief was identified, an unpaid watchman may choose either to swear or to go to court with the thief. A paid watchman goes to court with the thief and does not swear.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now quotes the ruling it mentioned in step 34. This ruling seems to clash with what רב נחמן did to רוניא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By this ruling, a שׁוֹמֵר חִנָּם whose item was robbed by force can just swear and walk away. רוניא was an unpaid watchman, yet רב נחמן made him liable and in effect forced him to deal with the thief. That looks like a contradiction.

keyTerms.meaning: Something beyond one's control, an unavoidable accident
He takes him (the thief) to court

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two watchmen. Only the unpaid one gets a choice. The paid one must go after the thief himself.

phrases.english: As Rav Huna bar Avin sent:
If it was stolen in a way beyond his control
and afterward the thief was identified,
if he is an unpaid watchman,
if he wants, he swears,
phrases.notes: He swears that he didn't misuse the item before it was stolen. Then the owner goes after the thief himself.

phrases.english: if he wants, he goes to court with him.
If he is a paid watchman,
he goes to court with him and does not swear.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the text of the ruling that step 34 said might contradict רב נחמן.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן's ruling holding the unpaid watchman רוניא liable
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If an unpaid watchman robbed by force may just swear, רוניא should have been exempt with an oath.

steps.title: רבא: help was nearby, so the watchman was negligent
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains that in רוניא's case, government men were standing nearby. Had he shouted, they would have saved him, so the robbery was not truly beyond his control.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: there, government men were standing around. If he had shouted, they would have come and rescued him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא resolves the contradiction by showing that the two cases are different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב הונא בר אבין's rule applies only to a real אוֹנֶס. רוניא could have called for help and didn't, so the loss came from his own negligence. That is why רב נחמן held him liable.
steps.whatToRemember: A robbery counts as אוֹנֶס only if the watchman truly could not stop it. If help was close enough to call, he is responsible.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the label 'robbery by force' alone doesn't exempt a שׁוֹמֵר. What matters is whether he could have prevented it.

phrases.english: Rava said:
There, men of the government
were standing around,
so that if he had raised his voice
they would have come and rescued him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in steps 34 and 35.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רוניא's robbery was a true אוֹנֶס, like the case of רב הונא בר אבין.
steps.terutzMaskana: רוניא could have called nearby officials, so he was negligent and liable.

steps.title: משנה: one wolf versus two wolves
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה rules that one wolf attacking the flock is not an אוֹנֶס, but two wolves are. רבי יהודה says that during a wave of wolf attacks, even one wolf counts as an אוֹנֶס.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: One wolf is not an unavoidable accident. Two wolves are. רבי יהודה says: in a time of wolf attacks, even one wolf is an unavoidable accident.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It sets out which animal attacks a shepherd is expected to fight off and which are beyond his control.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A shepherd is expected to drive off a single wolf, so if he fails he is responsible. Two wolves are too much for him. רבי יהודה adds that when wolves are swarming everywhere, even one wolf is too dangerous to resist.

keyTerms.meaning: A time when wolves are sent out, a wave of wolf attacks

phrases.english: MISHNAH:
One wolf is not an unavoidable accident.
Two wolves are an unavoidable accident.
Rabbi Yehuda says:
At a time of wolf attacks,
even one wolf is an unavoidable accident.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה after the previous discussion ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One wolf is not אוֹנֶס, two wolves are. According to רבי יהודה, even one wolf is אוֹנֶס during a time of wolf attacks.

steps.title: משנה: two dogs, and which direction they come from
steps.stepSummary: Two dogs are not an אוֹנֶס. ידוע הבבלי, quoting רבי מאיר, says it depends: dogs from one direction are not an אוֹנֶס, but dogs from two directions are.
steps.simpleTranslation: Two dogs are not an unavoidable accident. ידוע הבבלי says in the name of רבי מאיר: from one direction it is not an unavoidable accident, from two directions it is.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues its list, now with dogs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Dogs are weaker than wolves, so even two dogs can be driven off. ידוע הבבלי adds that if they attack from two sides at once, the shepherd can't guard both sides, so it counts as אוֹנֶס.

phrases.english: Two dogs are not an unavoidable accident.

phrases.aramaic: יָדוּעַ הַבַּבְלִי אוֹמֵר מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי מֵאִיר:
phrases.english: Yadua the Babylonian says in the name of Rabbi Meir:
From one direction, it is not an unavoidable accident;
from two directions, it is an unavoidable accident.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה's list, moving from wolves to dogs.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Two dogs are not אוֹנֶס. According to ידוע הבבלי, two dogs from two directions are אוֹנֶס.

steps.title: משנה: bandits and dangerous wild animals
steps.stepSummary: Bandits are an אוֹנֶס. A lion, bear, leopard, cheetah, or snake is also an אוֹנֶס.
steps.simpleTranslation: Bandits are an unavoidable accident. The lion, the bear, the leopard, the cheetah, and the snake are all unavoidable accidents.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה finishes its list with threats no shepherd can be expected to fight.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike a single wolf or dogs, bandits and these dangerous animals are beyond any shepherd's ability to resist. So a loss caused by them exempts the watchman. The גמרא will later explain that the bandits here are armed.
steps.whatToRemember: The משנה's test is simple: could a normal shepherd drive this threat away? If not, it is an אוֹנֶס.

phrases.english: Bandits: this is an unavoidable accident.
The lion, the bear, and the leopard
and the cheetah and the snake:
these are unavoidable accidents.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the משנה's list of threats.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Bandits and dangerous wild animals (lion, bear, leopard, cheetah, snake) are all אוֹנֶס.

steps.title: Beasts and bandits count only if they came on their own
steps.stepSummary: The משנה limits its earlier rule. Beasts and bandits are an אוֹנֶס only if they came by themselves. If the shepherd led the flock to where they gather, it is not an אוֹנֶס.
steps.simpleTranslation: When is this an אוֹנֶס? When they came on their own. But if he led the flock to a place of beast packs and bandits, it is not an אוֹנֶס.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה adds a limit to the list of dangers it just called אוֹנֶס (wolves, lions, bandits, and so on).
steps.deeperAnalysis: Something only counts as beyond his control if the shepherd did nothing to cause it. If he walked the flock right into danger, the loss is his own fault, so he must pay.

keyTerms.meaning: Packs or groups of wild animals

phrases.english: When?
When they came on their own.
But if he led them to a place
of packs of beasts and bandits,
it is not an unavoidable accident.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a limit to the list of אוֹנֶס cases in Step 39.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Beasts and bandits are an אוֹנֶס only when they came on their own. If the shepherd led the flock to them, he is liable.

steps.title: Natural death and cliffs: by itself or caused by the shepherd
steps.stepSummary: Natural death is an אוֹנֶס, but death from the shepherd wearing the animal out is not. An animal that climbs a cliff on its own and falls is an אוֹנֶס, but one the shepherd brought up the cliff is not.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it died normally, that is an אוֹנֶס. If he wore it out and it died, that is not an אוֹנֶס. If it climbed to the top of cliffs and fell, that is an אוֹנֶס. If he brought it up to the top of cliffs and it fell and died, that is not an אוֹנֶס.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives two more pairs of cases. In each pair, one case is the animal's own doing and the other is caused by the shepherd.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same idea from the last step runs through both pairs. The key question is who caused the loss. If the animal did it by itself, it is an אוֹנֶס. If the shepherd's actions led to it, he is responsible.

keyTerms.meaning: In its normal way (a natural death)
He wore it out or mistreated it
Tops of cliffs or steep rocks

steps.whatToRemember: In the משנה, a loss is an אוֹנֶס only when the shepherd did not bring it about. Leading the flock into danger, overworking the animal, or bringing it up a cliff all make him liable.

phrases.english: If it died in its normal way,
this is an unavoidable accident.
If he afflicted it and it died,
phrases.notes: Afflicted here means overworking it or not caring for it properly.

phrases.english: it is not an unavoidable accident.
If it climbed to the tops of cliffs and fell,
this is an unavoidable accident.
If he brought it up to the tops of cliffs
and it fell and died,
it is not an unavoidable accident.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same idea as Step 40 for natural death and falls.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Natural death and a fall the animal caused itself are an אוֹנֶס. Death from overwork, or a fall after the shepherd brought it up the cliff, are not.

steps.title: A ברייתא says one wolf is an אוֹנֶס
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the משנה with a ברייתא that says one wolf is an אוֹנֶס, while the משנה said one wolf is not.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: But it was taught in a ברייתא: one wolf is an אוֹנֶס!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins and right away points out that a ברייתא seems to contradict the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 37, the first opinion in the משנה said one wolf is not an אוֹנֶס, only two wolves are. A ברייתא says plainly that one wolf is an אוֹנֶס. So the גמרא asks how both can be right.

phrases.english: GEMARA
But was it not taught in a baraita:
one wolf is an unavoidable accident!
phrases.notes: This clashes with the משנה back in Step 37, which said one wolf is not an אוֹנֶס.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the משנה's wolf rule in Step 37 and raises a contradiction.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that one wolf is not an אוֹנֶס.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא directly says the opposite, that one wolf is an אוֹנֶס.

steps.title: The ברייתא follows רבי יהודה, during a wave of wolf attacks
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק answers that the ברייתא is talking about a time of many wolf attacks, and it follows רבי יהודה's opinion in the משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said: That ברייתא is talking about a time of wolf attacks, and it follows רבי יהודה.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק settles the contradiction by showing which situation, and which opinion, the ברייתא follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה already said in the משנה that during a wave of wolf attacks even one wolf is an אוֹנֶס. So the ברייתא is not arguing with the משנה. It matches רבי יהודה's view about that special time.

keyTerms.meaning: A wave or outbreak of wolf attacks

phrases.english: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak said:
That one is at a time of wolf attacks,
and it is the view of Rabbi Yehuda.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק הָהִיא בִּשְׁעַת מִשְׁלַחַת זְאֵבִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from Step 42.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the ברייתא to a special situation and links it to a specific תנא.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought the ברייתא says one wolf is always an אוֹנֶס, which would clash with the משנה.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is only about a wave of wolf attacks, following רבי יהודה. In ordinary times, the first opinion in the משנה stands.

steps.title: Why are bandits an אוֹנֶס? He could fight back
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why bandits count as an אוֹנֶס, since the shepherd could stand up to the bandit, one man against another.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said bandits are an אוֹנֶס. Why? Let one man stand up against the other man!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the משנה's rule that bandits are an אוֹנֶס.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A paid shepherd is supposed to protect the flock. If a bandit comes, it is just one man against another, so the shepherd should fight. Why should that be called beyond his control?

keyTerms.meaning: Let a man stand up against a man

phrases.english: Bandits: this is an unavoidable accident.
Why?
Let a man stand up against a man!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new line of the משנה, the rule about bandits.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that bandits are an אוֹנֶס.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: One bandit against one shepherd is an even fight, so the shepherd could defend the flock. The loss should not count as beyond his control.

steps.title: The משנה means armed bandits
steps.stepSummary: רב answers that the משנה is talking about armed bandits, whom a shepherd cannot be expected to fight.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: It is talking about armed bandits.
steps.whatsHappening: רב answers the question by narrowing which bandits the משנה means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An armed bandit is not an even fight, so the shepherd is not expected to risk his life against him. That is why the loss counts as truly beyond his control.
steps.whatToRemember: The bandits in the משנה are armed bandits. Against them the shepherd cannot fight back, so he is exempt.

phrases.english: Rav said:
With armed bandits.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from Step 44.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrows the case in the משנה.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought any bandit counts, even one the shepherd could beat in a fair fight.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה means armed bandits, whom the shepherd cannot reasonably fight, so it is a real אוֹנֶס.

steps.title: What if both the bandit and the shepherd are armed?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether an armed shepherd must fight an armed bandit, or whether this still counts as an אונס.
steps.simpleTranslation: A question was asked: if the bandit is armed and the shepherd is also armed, what is the law? Do we say it is just one man against another, so the shepherd should fight? Or maybe the bandit is ready to risk his life, and the shepherd is not?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא builds on רב's answer that armed bandits are an אונס. It asks what happens when the shepherd has weapons too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב's reason was that a shepherd cannot fight an armed man. If both are armed, they seem evenly matched, so maybe the shepherd should fight. On the other hand, the bandit came ready to kill or die, while the shepherd is just doing a job, so they are not really equal.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was asked before them (the חכמים)
Set a man against a man: they are evenly matched
He is ready to risk his life

phrases.english: A question was raised before them:
An armed bandit and an armed shepherd, what is the law?

phrases.aramaic: מִי אָמְרִינַן אוֹקֵי גַּבְרָא לַהֲדֵי גַּבְרָא,
phrases.english: Do we say: set one man against another man,
phrases.notes: He means that both have weapons, so it is a fair fight and the shepherd should stand up to him.

phrases.english: or perhaps: this one risks his life,
and that one does not risk his life?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows up on רב's answer (armed bandits) by asking about a case where the shepherd is armed too.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether an armed shepherd is expected to fight an armed bandit, or whether the attack is still an אונס.

steps.title: The bandit risks his life and the shepherd does not
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the bandit is ready to risk his life while the shepherd is not, so the shepherd does not have to fight.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense that the bandit is ready to risk his life, and the shepherd is not ready to risk his life.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its own question with simple reasoning. Even an armed shepherd does not have to fight an armed bandit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Having the same weapons does not make them equal. The bandit is willing to die for what he wants, but the shepherd is not expected to put his life on the line for the animals. So the attack stays an אונס, and the shepherd does not pay.

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense / it stands to reason

steps.whatToRemember: An armed bandit is an אונס even if the shepherd is armed too, because the bandit is ready to risk his life and the shepherd is not.

phrases.english: It stands to reason that this one risks his life,
and that one does not risk his life.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 46 by choosing the second side.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The bandit risks his life and the shepherd does not, so the shepherd is not expected to fight even when armed. The attack remains an אונס.

steps.title: אביי's case: the shepherd who taunts a thief
steps.stepSummary: אביי begins describing a case to רבא: a shepherd meets a thief, insults him, and tells him where the shepherds sit.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to רבא: Suppose a shepherd found a thief and said to him: "You stinking thief! We sit in such and such a place."
steps.whatsHappening: This line is a setup. אביי is laying out a new case for רבא, and the actual question comes in the next lines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the shepherd is not just a victim. He insults the thief and tells him exactly where the shepherds will be. The question that is coming will be about how that changes the shepherd's responsibility.

phrases.english: Abaye said to Rava:
If the shepherd found him and said to him:
phrases.notes: "Him" is a thief. The גמרא does not say so directly, but the shepherd's words show it.

phrases.english: You stinking thief!
In such and such a place we sit,
phrases.notes: "We" means the shepherds. The sentence keeps going on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new case about thieves, this time where the shepherd's own words are part of the story.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The case is still being laid out. The question about the shepherd's responsibility comes on the next amud.
